prerequisites: Elementary concepts of chemistry - normal prior knowledge from secondary education (A.S.O.)
Participation certificate in a benchmarking test for Bachelor of Engineering Science programs

learning_outcomes.text: Know the (sub)atomic structure of matter (up to the level of the nucleus with protons and neutrons and the surrounding electron cloud).
Understand the construction of the Periodic Table of Elements from the (sub)atomic structure of matter.
Explain and predict periodically varying properties such as atomic radius, electronegativity, etc., from the (sub)atomic structure of matter.
Understand and predict the different chemical bond types (ionic, covalent, metallic) and their properties.
Be able to draw Lewis structures and derive the symmetry and geometry of molecules.
Understand and predict intermolecular particle forces and interactions.
Explain and predict macroscopic properties of matter such as solubility, polarity, and hardness.
Understand and quantify the behavior of pure substances (gases, liquids, and solids) (e.g., ideal gas law).

Understand and quantify the behavior of homogeneous mixtures (gas and liquid) (e.g., Dalton's Law, Raoult's Law), including colligative properties (such as boiling point elevation, freezing point depression).
Be able to describe and quantify chemical transformations via the associated stoichiometry (i.e., balancing reactions).
Be able to apply concepts such as reaction extent and different types of yields.
Know, calculate, and apply the criteria for spontaneity of processes, derived from Gibbs free energy (e.g., for examples of explosives).
Understand the empirical approach and thermodynamic foundation of the Law of Mass Action (Guldberg and Waage) in relation to chemical equilibrium.
Recognize the importance of mixing entropy, which makes all chemical reactions equilibrium reactions.
Know and be able to apply the concept of equilibrium constant and reaction quotient.
Know and be able to apply Le Chatelier-Braun's principle.
Know the ammonia production process and place it in the context of the application(s) of Le Chatelier-Braun's principle.
Know and be able to apply the T- and P-dependence of equilibrium (including Van 't Hoff's Law).
Know and be able to apply the different acid-base theories.

Be able to derive the pH formula and, more importantly, calculate it for all types of mixtures (i.e., single acid or base, multiple acids or bases, salts, and acid-base neutralizations including buffers and titration reactions).
Know and recognize acid-base applications.
Master the two tables of solubility perfectly.
Understand how the solubility of salts can be influenced and be able to apply this yourself.
Be able to work quantitatively with (combinations of) precipitation, acid-base, and complex formation reactions (which reactions occur to what extent) using the respective stability constants.
Be able to discuss the given examples and recognize or apply the underlying principles in other examples.
Be able to determine the oxidation state of all elements in a molecule or ion.
Be able to balance any given redox reaction using the provided step-by-step plan.
Know most common oxidizing and reducing agents with some applications.
Know the working principle of a galvanic cell (and batteries) and an electrolytic cell.
Be able to predict which redox reaction(s) will occur in a specific environment using a given table of standard reduction potentials.
Understand and be able to apply Nernst's law.
Know and be able to use the relationship between Nernst's law and Gibbs free energy and the equilibrium constant K.
Understand the given examples and production processes and recognize or apply the underlying principles in other examples.
Be able to recognize gas formation reactions, predict them, and understand that they will likely lead to reactions that proceed well.
Be able to discuss the given integrated applications (hard water / limestone caves - Mg production - dissolution of gold) and recognize or apply the underlying principles in other examples.

syllabus_topics: MATTER (BOOK 1)
Atoms – subatomic structure – construction of the Periodic Table of Mendeleev
Periodically varying properties: ionic radii – atomic radii – ionization energy – electron affinity – electronegativity
Chemical bonding: ionic – covalent – metallic bonding: qualitative, classical description
Different types of interparticle forces and interactions (with solubility of salts as an important application)
Behavior of pure substances: gases, liquids, and solids:
Equations of state for ideal and non-ideal gases (van der Waals)
Surface tension – viscosity
Homogeneous mixtures
Description of homogeneous mixtures – concentration quantities and conversions
Behavior of ideal gas mixtures – partial pressure – Dalton's Law – conversions
Behavior of liquid mixtures – ideal mixtures – Raoult's Law
Vapor pressure lowering – boiling point elevation – freezing point depression – osmotic pressure
Heterogeneous mixtures
Requirements for phase equilibrium of mixtures
Liquid-vapor equilibrium for ideal mixtures (Raoult's Law)
CHEMICAL REACTIONS AND EQUILIBRIUM (BOOK 2)
Chemical transformations: stoichiometry + definitions: extent of reaction etc.
Criteria for spontaneity of processes + Gibbs free energy
Calculation of reaction quantities
The Law of Mass Action (Guldberg and Waage): empirical approach and thermodynamic foundation
T- and P- dependence of equilibrium (including Van 't Hoff's Law)
Le Chatelier-Braun's Principle
Calculation of equilibrium composition in mixtures of reacting substances
Equilibrium of gas reactions
Equilibria in aqueous solutions:
Acid-base reactions: the concept of pH – acid-base theories – pH calculations of mixtures of acids, bases, and salts – buffer mixtures – titrations – applications
Precipitation reactions: solubility product – equilibrium calculations – influencing solubility – applications
Complexation reactions: stability constant – equilibrium calculations – influence of pH – applications
Redox reactions: oxidation state – balancing – electrochemical series of metals – standard redox potential – galvanic cell/batteries – electrolysis – Nernst's Law – applications
Integrated applications: hard water / limestone caves – production of Mg
Seminar 1: General basic concepts (homework)
Seminar 2: Concentration quantities and reaction equations
Seminar 3: Reaction equations and ideal gas law
Seminar 4: Review exercises (in preparation for interim test)
Seminar 5: Reactions: redox reactions
Seminar 6: Reactions: precipitation, acid-base, gas formation reactions
Seminar 7: Thermodynamic reaction quantities (homework)
Seminar 8: Chemical equilibrium in gas mixtures
Seminar 9: Chemical equilibrium in aqueous solutions 1: solutions of acids or bases
Seminar 10: Chemical equilibrium in aqueous solutions 2: acid-base neutralization; buffer mixtures
Seminar 11: Chemical equilibrium in aqueous solutions 3: precipitation reactions and complexation
Seminar 12: Chemical equilibrium in aqueous solutions 4: exam questions
assessment_rules: An interim test is organized. If the student passes the interim test and achieves a better result on it than on the exam in the next exam period, the interim test result will be factored into the final result with a ratio of one-fourth for the interim test and three-fourths for the exam. This recalculation does not apply to results obtained in the third exam period. The written exam consists of a theory part and an exercise part, with a minimum of 7/20 required on the exercise part. Failure to achieve 7/20 on the exercise part in January means the student cannot pass via the interim test correction. During resits, no recalculation of the interim test score will be applied.
